front: Why is the demand for health care called a 'derived demand'?
back: Because what people really want is health. Health care is demanded mainly as a means to produce health.

front: What does a price elasticity of demand of -0.2 mean?
back: Elasticity $\varepsilon = \frac{\%\Delta Q}{\%\Delta P} = -0.2$: a 10% rise in price lowers the quantity demanded by about 2%. Demand is inelastic: it reacts only a little to price.

front: Name three non-price factors that affect the demand for health care.
back: For example: health status, income, insurance coverage, time costs (travel and waiting), and information about one's own condition.

front: What is moral hazard in health insurance?
back: Insured people tend to use more care (or take less care to stay healthy) because insurance lowers the price they face.

front: What is a deductible?
back: An amount the insured person pays out of pocket each year before the insurance starts paying.

front: Coinsurance vs copayment: what is the difference?
back: Coinsurance is a percentage of the cost of care (e.g. 20%). A copayment is a fixed amount per service (e.g. 10 euros per visit).

front: What does health economics study?
back: How scarce resources are used in health and healthcare, including choices by patients, providers, insurers and governments.

front: Why is economic analysis relevant even when health is described as 'priceless'?
back: Because producing and protecting health still uses scarce resources, so choices involve trade-offs and opportunity costs.

front: What is the difference between healthcare expenditure per capita and healthcare expenditure as a share of GDP?
back: Per-capita expenditure relates spending to population; HCE/GDP relates spending to the size of the whole economy.

front: What is opportunity cost?
back: The value of the best alternative that is given up when a choice is made.

front: What does marginal analysis ask?
back: What happens when one additional unit of an activity, input or resource is added or removed.

front: What is information asymmetry in healthcare?
back: A situation where the parties do not have the same information; for example, a physician usually knows more than a patient about diagnosis and treatment.

front: Why does uncertainty make insurance important in healthcare?
back: People do not know exactly when illness will occur, what care will be needed, how much it will cost or what the outcome will be, so insurance can protect against uncertain financial losses.

front: What is an externality?
back: A cost or benefit from an action that affects people other than the person making the decision.

front: Efficiency and equity: what is the difference?
back: Efficiency concerns how well resources are used; equity concerns fairness in how resources, opportunities or outcomes are distributed.

front: What are the three government roles highlighted in Session 1?
back: Regulator, insurer and provider.

front: Who are the three actors in the medical-care triad?
back: Patient, provider and insurer/government.

front: What is financial intermediation in healthcare?
back: Financing care through a third party, such as an insurer or government, instead of paying the provider entirely at the point of use.

front: Why can total healthcare value be high while marginal productivity is low?
back: Healthcare may create large overall health gains, yet an additional euro of spending can produce only a small extra health gain when many valuable interventions are already funded.

front: Which four broad health-system models are used as a teaching framework in Session 1?
back: Beveridge, Bismarck, American and cash-based.

front: Name the four economic features emphasized when asking why healthcare is different.
back: Information asymmetry, uncertainty, externalities and equity concerns.

front: What does a demand curve show?
back: The quantity consumers are willing and able to buy at each price, holding other determinants constant.

front: Movement along a demand curve vs a shift: what is the difference?
back: A price change causes movement along a given demand curve. A change in another determinant, such as income, health status or the price of a related service, can shift the curve.

front: What is willingness to pay (WTP)?
back: The maximum amount a buyer is willing to pay for a good or service; it measures how much the buyer values it.

front: What is consumer surplus?
back: Willingness to pay minus the amount actually paid.

front: What is a marginal consumer?
back: The active buyer with the lowest willingness to pay at the market price; the marginal consumer receives zero consumer surplus.

front: Name four determinants of how price-sensitive demand may be.
back: Share of income spent on the good, availability of substitutes, necessity versus luxury, and the time horizon such as urgent versus elective care.

front: How can worsening health status affect healthcare demand?
back: People may demand more healthcare at every price; the lecture also illustrates demand becoming steeper when people are sicker.

front: Why can observational estimates of healthcare demand be biased?
back: People choose insurance partly according to health risk, so out-of-pocket prices are not randomly assigned. Unobserved health differences can be mistaken for a price effect.

front: Why are randomized experiments useful for estimating healthcare demand?
back: Random assignment creates groups that are statistically comparable, making differences in use easier to attribute to the assigned price or insurance condition.

front: What are the two major randomized experiments emphasized in Session 2?
back: The RAND Health Insurance Experiment and the Oregon Medicaid Experiment.

front: What broad result do RAND and Oregon support about healthcare demand?
back: Healthcare demand is downward sloping: when the price patients face is higher, use tends to be lower.

front: Is healthcare demand perfectly inelastic?
back: No. The lecture presents healthcare demand as inelastic overall, but still responsive to price.

front: What is arc elasticity?
back: A unit-free measure of responsiveness calculated between two price-quantity points using midpoint percentage changes.

front: What is the full price of a healthcare visit?
back: The monetary price plus other costs such as travel expenses and the opportunity cost of time spent travelling, waiting and receiving care.

front: Why can time costs matter more when insurance is generous?
back: Insurance can reduce the monetary price paid by the patient, while waiting and travel time remain. Time costs therefore become a larger share of the full price.

front: What is a fixed indemnity?
back: A fixed amount paid by the insurer for a particular covered service, leaving the patient responsible for the remaining price.

front: What is coinsurance?
back: The fraction of the healthcare bill that remains payable by the patient; the insurer pays the rest.

front: What is a copayment?
back: A fixed amount the patient pays for each unit of healthcare use, such as a fixed amount per visit.

front: What is a deductible?
back: An amount the patient must pay toward medical bills before insurance reimbursement begins.

front: What policy concern does Session 2 raise about cost-sharing?
back: Higher cost-sharing can reduce healthcare use without necessarily distinguishing between high-value and low-value care.
